Power consumers in Delhi 
1092. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that on an average, 30 lakh billed power 
consumers in Delhi had paid about Rs. 5000/- this year for power that others 
have stolen; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the billed consumers had to pay for 
guaranteeing a 16 percent return on any investments private distributors make; 
and 
(c) if so, who is responsible for putting the interests of innocent 
consumer at the whims and wishes of private power distribution companies 
and what safeguards would be initiated to check it? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
The electricity sector in Delhi is a regulated business and it is governed by an 
independent regulator, Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC). The 
consumer is required to pay the chargesfof the consumption of electricity based 
upon the tariff approved by the DERC from time to time. While fixing tariff 
the level of Aggregate Technical & Commercial losses is also taken into 
consideration. In some of the pockets AT&C loss level is still more than 
50%. 
(b) As per the policy directions of Government of NCT of Delhi, 16% 
return on the issued and paid up capital and free reserves (excluding consumer 
contribution and revaluation reserves but including share premium and 
retained profits outstanding at the end of any particular 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
year) is admissible to the licensee prov ided that such share capital and free 
reserves have been invested into fixed or any other assets, which have been put 
into beneficial use for the purpose of electricity distribution and retail supply and 
provided further that such investment of such share capital and free reserves has 
the approval of the Commi ssion. These policy directions are applicable only 
for first five years of privatization beginning 1st July, 2002. 16% return is 
available only when the licensee has achieved the committed levels of AT&C 
loss reduction. Further the distribution licensee's returns are adversely affected 
if it fails to achieve the set targets. 
(c) For safeguarding the interests of consumers, the DERC, inter alia, 
monitors the following:— 
• Loss reduction. 
• Properly incurred expenses in approving tariff 
• Performance standards. 
• Consumer grievance redressal.

1095. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the steps taken so far by the Central and State Governments, including the 
State Electricity Boards to introduce open access in the power generation, transmission 
and dustribution sector; 
(b) the private sectors response, so far, in the transmission sector, >n ins power 
generation sector, especially the hydro-power generation;

sector, where they have direct inter-face with the poor consumer and collect easy 
money? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) The 
Electricity Act, 2003 has delicensed generation. It provides for open access in 
transmission from the very beginning. The Act provides for phased introduction of 
open access in distribution by the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs). 
The Act provides that the State Commission shall, not later than 27th January, 2009, by 
regulations, provide such open access to all consumers who require a supply of 
electricity where the maximum power to be made available at any time exceeds one 
megawatt. 
The Tariff Policy suggests that in whichever states the situation so permits, the 
Regulatory Commissions should introduce open access even prior to this deadline. The 
policy lays down the methodology for computation of cross subsidy surcharge. 
The National Electricity Policy stresses on the need to provide facilitative 
frame-work by the Regulatory Commissions for non-discriminative open 
access. 
The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) had already issued 
regulations on grant of open access in inter-state transmission. At the State level, 19 
SERCs have issued final regulations and 2 SERCs have issued draft regulations on open 
access in distribution. 
As per information available, applications for grant of open access in distribution 
have been received in various States and seven cases of

Revised structure of APDRP 
1101. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to restructure the Accelerated Power 
Development & Reforms Programme (APDRP) with an outlay of Rs. 40,000 
crore under the Tenth Five Year Plan; 
(b) if so, the details and main features of the APDRP; 
(c) on what lines the programme was sought to be restructured, and the 
revised structure and other details of the restructured programme; and 
(d) the objects sought to be ach ieved under the restructured 
programme? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
122 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) and (c) Keeping in view the sensitivity of the need to reform and 
revitalizing of the power sector, changes have been incorporated in the 
implementation of Accelerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) from time to time. The changes have been based not only 
on the requirement but also on the basis of feedback received from various 
stakeholders in the power sector. They are: 
(i) APDRP was originally started as Accelerated Power Development 
Programme (APDP) in 2000-01, with emphasis on upgradation of 
sub-transmission and distribution network and also on renovation 
and modernization/life extension/uprating of old power plants (thermal 
and hydel). 
(ii) Based on the resolutions passed in the Chief Ministers' conference 
held on March 3, 2001 and recommendations of Deepak Parekh 
Committee on Staie specific reforms APDP was rechristened as 
APDRP during 2002-03 with focus on concentrated zones i.e. 
industrial and urban areas. Incentive component was introduced in 
2002-03 to encourage the utilities to reduce their cash losses. 
(iii) To make the programme more effective, the following measures were 
initiated: 
♦ the utilities were asked to sign Memorandum of Agreement 
(MOA), to commit improvements in set of benchmark 
parameters. 
♦ Linking of securitisation under Tripartite Agreement to secure 
CPSUs dues for assistance under APDRP. 
♦ A massive programme for training of utility personnel. 
♦ Ranking of SEBs/utilities by independent agencies viz CRISIL 
&ICRA. 
♦ Dissemination of best practices amongst the utilities through 
national level workshops. 
♦ Appointing agencies like TERI (The Energy & Resources 
Institute), SBI Capital, Tata Consultancy Services, Indian 
Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIMA) and ASCI 
(Administrative Staff College of India), Hyderabad to evaluate 
APDRP projects. 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
The main features of programme are to reduce Aggregate Technical and Commercial 
(AT & C) losses; to bring about commercial viability; to reduce outages and interruptions; 
and to increase consumer satisfaction. The programme envisages an investment 
component that covers strengthening and upgradation of sub-transmission and 
distribution system with twenty five percent grant and an incentive component as grant 
to states/utilities that reduce cash losses with 2000-01 as the base year. 
Thus, restructuring the Accelerated Power Development and Reforms 
Programme (APDRP) is a continuous process not only to fine-tune the parameters of 
performance of the power utilities but also to motivate the power utilities to become 
commercially viable. 
(d) APDRP will the continue to focus on reducing AT&C losses, improve 
commercial viability of the Utilities, reducing outages & interruptions and to 
improve consumer satisfaction.

Monsoon forecasting agencies 
1107. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Indian Meterological Department and the CSIR 
for Mathematical modelling and computer simulation have given two different 
monsoon forecasts; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether the gadgets used for predicting monsoon in India are primitive and 
require change and the reasons forwhich these two agencies don't share their expertise? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
Yes, Sir. The mandate for issuing long range monsoon forecast for the country rests with 
India Meteorological Department (IMD). IMD uses a statistical model for monsoon 
forecast. Centre for Mathematical Modelling and Computer Simulation (C-MMACS) is 
conducting studies on monsoon forecast and uses a dynamical model on experimental basis. 
Studies have shown that dynamical models have not evolved to a stage where they can 
simulate the year to year monsoon rainfall realistically. 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
Therefore, IMD which has been historically depending on the statistical model 
have not yet adopted dynamical model for making forecast. More test and 
research work is required to switchover to dynamical model for making 
monsoon forecast by IMD. 
(b) C-MMACS issued fo recasts for June, July and August months 
separately. Prediction made by C-MMA CS for June rainfall was below 
normal by 34%, prediction for July 2005 was12% below normal and for 
AugusJ, 13% above normal. Actual ra infall in June 2005 was 12% below 
normal, in July 14% above normal and in August 27% below normal. 
IMD's forecast for the seasonal rainfall over the country as a whole was 
2% below normal which was very close to actual seasonal rainfall (1% below 
normal). 
(c) No, Sir. IMD make use of all available parameters which using 
statistical model which has been validated over the years. In addition, 
IMD also uses a dynamical model in experimental mode to obtain more 
insights to the spatial distribution of rainfall. IMD is continuously engaged 
in improvement of forecast systems. IMD also consults all other research 
institutions including C-MMACS before issuing forecasts.

neuroscience and establish linkages with national and international

1110. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: W ill the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Nanotechnology has far reaching impact on electronics 
and computing, data storage, materials and manufacturing, energy, environment, healthcare, 
medicine and transportation; 
(b) whether Government propose to conduct any research and training 
programme in Nanotechnology and if so, what are the target areas of research; and 
(c) whether Government propose to formulate any policy guideline in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Government is fully aware of the impact and implications of Nanoscience 
and Nanotechnology. Various Ministries/Departments such as Department of Science 
and Technology (DST), Defence Research and Development Organization (DRDO), 
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Department of Biotechnology 
(DBT) have been supporting research projects and some facilities in 
Nanoscience and Technology. DST has launched a national programme titled "Nano 
Science and Technology Initiative (NSTI)' in October 2001. The programme focuses 
at overall research and development in nanoscience and technology with vigour so 
that India can become a significant player in the area and contribute to the development 
of new 
136 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
technologies besides carrying out basic research at the frontiers. The initiative includes 
R&D programme, strengthening characterization and infrastructure! facilities, creation of 
centres of excellence, generate trained manpower, interface between educational 
institutions and industry for applications etc. Target areas of R&D include both basic 
research in nano science in areas such as DNAchips, molecular electronics, quantum 
structures including dots, nanotubes & wires, nanobiology, nanofabrication, 
nanolithography and applied technology oriented research in ares such as composite 
materials with high strength-to-weight ratio, new biomedical solutions for chronic 
diseases, new drugs and targeted drug delivery, affordable nanoscale miniaturized 
medical diagnostic and treatment devices, improvements to computing, sensing, 
communications, data storage etc. On the manpower development front, advanced schools 
and International/National symposia and training workshops for research 
scholars/students have been held. Recognizing the growing scientific importance 
and emerging technological opportunities in this area of research and to formulate a 
policy guideline, a national-level consultation among scientists and technologists and S&T 
agencies (namely DST, DRDO, CSIR, DBT) promoting this area was organized. This 
consultation process has resulted in a major National programme titled 'Nano Science & 
Technology Mission (Nano Mission)'. The Nano Mission includes components like 
R&D programme, development of educational resources, establishing 
centres of nanotechnology, technology transfer though mechanisms such as public-private 
partnerships, skilled workforce and to support responsible development of 
nanotechnology.

Monsoon prediction 
1114. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact there is no improvement in the predictions of monsoon in 
India since early 1930s; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have studied the recurring failures in predicting 
droughts and floods; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
and (b) No, Sir. India Meteorological Department (IMD) has been issuing operational 
long range forecasts based on objective statistical models since late 1920s. 
From 1924 to 1987, India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued forecasts 
for two broad homogeneous region (NW India and Peninsula). During this period, on 
an average, the percentage of correct forecasts ranged between 58% to 63%. Since 1988, 
IMD has prepared forecasts for southwest monsoon rainfall over the country as a whole. 
During the period 1988—2005, all the forecasts (for the country as a whole) were 
generally correct except in drought year of 2002 and 2004, when rainfall received 
were in the deficient category against forecast of normal rainfall. It may be mentioned, that 
no operational forecasting group (either in India or abroad) could predict the droughts of 
2002 and 2004. IMD's forecasts for 2005 southwest monsoon rainfall was proved 
correct. 
(c) and (d) There are no techniques available at present to predict droughts in 
advance. They are being dynamically monitored. IMD provides necessary inputs on rainfall 
distribution of all meteorological subdivisions to the concerned agencies during the 
monsoon season. This helps in mobilizing resources to combat the evolving drought 
scenarios. 
IMD also provides necessary meteorological inputs to Central Water Commission, 
which is the nodal agency for flood forecasting. However, forecast of heavy rainfall which 
may lead to flood situations is done only in short range time scale. 
140 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
For improving Long rage forecasting of monsoon rainfall, India 
Meteorological Department has been making critical review of its predictions 
regularly, especially after the failure in 2002 and 2004. IMD has taken the following 
major steps to improve its monsoon prediction capability. 
• Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore is collaborating with IMD and helping 
to implement a dynamical prediction system using the mathematical model 
developed at the Experimental Climate Prediction Centre, scripps Institute of 
Oceanography, USA. This model has shown reasonable skill in predicting 
monsoon rainfall over India. Using this model, experimental forecasts 
were prepared for the 2005 southwest monsoon rainfall. However, 
more.quality tests and research work are required before the model can be put 
to use for operation of work. 
• As statistical models outperform dynamical models at present, IMD has 
developed many new statistical models with the aim to replace existing 
operational statistical models. These new statistical models have shown 
improved skill but have to be tested for a couple of years more before their use in 
operational mode. 
(e) Doesn't arise.

AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI G.K. VASAN): (a) and 
(b) In the past, National Accounts Statistics were revised decennially using 
the information on working force from the Population Census. However, in the 
previous series of national accounts with the base year 1993-94 (introduced in 
February, 1999), the workforce data from the Quinquennial Employment and 
Unemployment Survey, 1993-94 conducted by the National sample survey 
Organisation (NSSO) in its 50th round was used, as it was observed that data on 
Worker Participation Rate (WPR) as captured by the NSS better than that 
through the Population Census. In continuation with this practice, the Central 
Statistical Organisation (CSO) introduced the new series of national accounts 
(base year 1999-2000) using the WPR data available from the next NSS 55th

1137. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to give top priority to the improvement 
of water management system in urban areas besides sanitation and development 
of slums; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
(c) the steps taken or proposed to be taken by Government to 
implement the progress of water management system in urban areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIAJAY MAKEN): (a) to  (c) Yes, Sir. This Ministry 
gives top priority for improvement of water management system in urban areas 
to ensure an efficient and sustained water supply system and services. Top 
priority is also attached to sector reforms, namely, institutional and financial 
reforms including capacity building to ensure efficient management of water 
supply system in urban areas. Model building bye-laws have been prepared 
and circulated to State Governments by the Town & Country Planning 
Organization to include water conserva tion measures such as rain water 
harvesting, reuse and recycle of waste water in urban areas. A Manual on 
operation & Maintenance of Water Supply Systems has been published by 
Ministry of Urban Development for planning and designing various 
components of water supply systems to help personnel involved in execution 
and maintenance of water supply proj ects. The Manual also deals with 
qualitative aspects of treated water for drinking purpose. 
Ministry of Urban Development has already launched Jawaharlal Nehru 
National Urban Renewal Mission and Urban Infrastructure Development 
Scheme for Small and Medium Towns for providing reform-linked central 
assistance to cities & towns. The main objective is to secure effective linkages 
between asset creation and asset management so that the water supply services 
created in the cities are not only maintained efficiently but also become self-
sustaining over a period of time. Some of the mandatory reforms to be 
undertaken at ULB and/or state leve l are adoption of modern, accrual-based 
double entry system of accounting, introduction of system of e-governance 
using IT applications, levy of reasonable user charges with the objective that 
full cost of operation and maintenance of recurring cost is collected, etc. Some 
of the optional reforms to be implemented at the state and/or ULB level are 
revision of bye-laws to make rain water harvesting mandatory in all 
buildings, adoption of water conservation measures, structural reforms, 
public private partnership etc. These reforms are expected to improve water 
management system in urban areas.

introduced?

EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) and (b) 
The main thrust of the revised strategy of urban renewal, including providing basic services 
to the urban poor, is to ensure improvement in urban governance so that Urban Local 
Bodies (ULBs) and para-statal agencies become financially sound with enhanced credit 
rating and ability to access market capital for undertaking new programmes and expansion of 
services. In this improved environment, public-private participation models for 
provisioning of various services would also become feasible. Accordingly, under the Sub-

Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) launched on 3rd December 2005, projects with 
private sector participation will be encouraged, as this will help leverage private capital and 
bring in efficiency. The Integrated Housing & Slum Development Programme 
(IHSDP) that was launched along with the JNNURM, also seeks to enhance public 
and private investments in housing and infrastructure! development in urban 
areas.

1173.    SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
SHRI BALAVANT alias BALAPTE: 
Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Sports Federations have been allotted funds for improving the 
performance and practices of sports persons;

them during the last two years; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether Government have taken any action against such federations for 
misutilisation of funds during the last three years; 
(f) if so, the details thereof; and 
(g) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) The funds allotted to the recognised National Sports 
Federations for improving the performance of sports persons/teams during the last three 
years are detailed in the Statement. (See below) 
(c) to (g) National Sports Federations (NSFs) are autonomous societies 
registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860. The Government of India 
provides assistance to recognized NSFs for organizing national and international 
events in India, participation in international tournaments abroad, procurement of 
equipment, training of national teams/sports-persons under Indian/foreign coaches, etc. 
There have been some complaints against NSFs about misuse of funds received from the 
Government. Any complaint against any NSF about misuse of funds etc. is processed 
promptly after ascertaining the comments of the NSF concerned. To ensure proper 
utilization of Government assistance, utilization certificates and statements of 
accounts duly audited by chartered accountants are required to be submitted and further 
assistance is released only on receipt of these documents. Further, this Ministry has issued 
sanction for audit through the Comptroller & Auditor General of India of NSFs getting 
assistance exceeding Rs. one crore in a year.

Need for augmenting public preparedness towards disaster 
management 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA (Maharashtra): Sir, no doubt role of 
the Government in any disaster management is of primary 
importance, but unless people are fully prepared to contribute their 
best, desired results cannot be achieved. While dissemination of 
information starts from Government quarters, prior drills to fully 
acquaint and adequately prepare the community to handle entire 
action at the grass roots is a decisive 
222 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
factor. These include quick evacuation,  identification of safe buildings 
speedy outsourcing of m edical facilities, administration of first aid, 
centralization of in-bound relief materials and their efficient and 
equitable distribution to avoid occurrence of any stampede, community 
cohabitation with special stress on hygiene to eliminate outbreak any 
disease. After initial relief and rehabilitation measures have been 
taken care of, the next step is restor ation of livelihood, especially for 
fishermen, self-employed artisans, small and marginal farmers, petty 
traders, etc. For them, custom-m ade measures are required to be 
initiated with their active coop eration and that of banks and other 
philanthropic bodies, who either give outright aid in kind or cash, or 
soft interest-free loans, etc. The spot functional-level Government 
officials be given maximum decentralisation of power to take quick and 
scenario-based decisions based on local needs. If an attempt is made 
to codify such measures to be followed, indicating modalities how 
public cooperation is to be enlisted and how general awareness is to 
be created, it will be a good beginning to effectively tackle natural 
disasters and minimise human suffering.

Increase in number of farmers committing suicide in Vidarbha. 
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Sir, I rise to 
make this Special Mention to bring to the attention of the House and 
the Government the fact that the number of farmers committing 
suicide in Vidarbha region this year in Maharashtra State has reached 
the figure of 
299. 
A farmer from village Sarandi, taluka Lakhandur, district 
Bhandara, had taken loan for purchasing a tractor. The debt had 
swollen to over Rs. 3 lakhs. Desper ate at the inability to repay the 
loan and unable to see the humiliation of the recovery proceedings, 
he immolated himself after drenching himself with kerosene. He 
suffered 85 per cent burns. A widow and three sons survive him. 
In the 299th case, another farmer, from Pimpalkhunta village in 
Dhamangaon taluka of Amaravati district, consumed poison at around 
quarter past five in the morning of the 24th February. He suffered under 
the burden of a loan of barely Rs. 50,000. He owned fifteen acres of 
land. His fields were attacked by wild boars. Consequently, his 
production was limited to barely 10 quintal of cotton and nine quintal 
of soya bean. He had three eligible daughters and was worried about 
getting them settled. He expired at around 7 o' clock in the morning. 
His widow, son and four daughters survive him. 
By the time that I am making this Special Mention, the 
number of suicides in Vidarbha, this year, would have well crossed ihe 
300-mark. I, therefore, request the Government to take some strong 
measures immediately to help the farmers. 
GOVERNMENT BILL 
The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Bill, 
2005 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN:   The hon. Minister will now move 
the Bill. 
224 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHR! 
MURLI DEORA):   Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill to provide for the establishment of Petroleum 
and Natural Gas Regulatory Board to regulate the 
refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, 
marketing and sale of petroleum, petroleum products and 
natural gas excluding production of crude oil and natural 
gas so as to protect the interests of consumers and 
entities engaged in specified activities relating to 
petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas and to 
ensure uninterrupted and adequate supply of petroleum, 
petroleum products and natural gas in all parts of the 
country and to promote competitive markets and for 
matters connected therewith or  incidental thereto, be 
taken into consideration.'' 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, my predecessor had Introduced a Bill 
entitled The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board 6tt, 2005' in 
this august House on 21" December , 2005. I seek the leave of the 
House for taking up this Bill for consideration. 
Before I come to the specifics of this Bill, I would like to state 
briefly the importance of the oil and gas sector in our growing economy. 
Energy is an essential requirement for economic development and it is 
an important pre-requistte for improving the quality of life of the people.   
At present, in the primary commercial energy mix of our country, coal, oil 
and gas constitute about 51 per cent, 36 per cent and 9 per cent 
respectively, with the balance four  per cent being met by the other 
sources.  As per the Hydrocarbon Vaion-2025, the combined share of 
oil and gas in the total energy mix in 2025 is likely to remain at the 
current level of 45 per cent. Our economy is poised to grow by over 8 
per cent during 2005-06 and this trend of robust growth is projected to 
continue in the foreseeable future. We import more than 70 per cent of 
our crude oil requirements to meet the dom estic demand of petroleum 
products. Further, at present, about only 50 per cent of the estimated 
gas demand is met by indigenous production. Thus, meeting the oil 
and gas requirements of our growing economy is a d aunting task. The 
National Common Minimum Programme emphasizes the need to put in 
place policies to enhance the country's energy security. The efforts 
made by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas in enhancing the oil 
and gas security of the country include - facilitating increase in domestic 
oil and gas production under the New Exploration and Licensing 
Policy, 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
acquiring oil and gas acreages abroad, facilitating LNG imports, taking 
initiative to import gas through transnational pipelines, diversifying 
crude oil supply sources, and taking steps to build strategic crude oil 
storage. 
The different sectors of the Indian economy have 
progressively moved towards the market-driven regimes in the past 
few years. In the sectors requir ing regulatory intervention, viz., 
electricity, telecom, etc., statutor y regulators have been established. 
Not only has this facilitated the much-needed investments in these 
sectors and their orderly growth , the consumers have benefited on 
account of availability of better serv ices and products at competitive 
prices. 
Through this Bill, the Government is envisaging to set up a 
statutory downstream petroleum a nd natural gas regulator with the 
following main objectives: 
to regulate the refining, processing, storage, 
transportation, distribution, marketing and sale of 
petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas so as to 
protect the interests of consumers and entities engaged in 
specified activities relating to petroleum, petroleum 
products and natural gas; 
to ensure uninterrupted  and adequate supply of 
petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas in all parts 
of the country; 
to promote competitive markets. 
Sir, earlier, in the 13 th Lok Sabha, the then Minister for 
Petroleum and Natural Gas had introduced "The Petroleum 
Regulatory Board Bill, 2002" in the Lok Sabha on the 6 th May, 2002. 
On the 17 th May, 2002, the Bill was referred to the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Petroleum and Chemicals for examination 
and report. The Committee presented its report to the Lok Sabha 
about a year later, on the 8lh May, 2003, recommending that the Bill be 
passed, subject to their recommendations and observations. The 
official amendments, as proposed by the Committee, were introduced 
by the earlier. Government in the 14th session of the 13th Lok Sabha in 
December, 2003. However, the Bill could not be taken up for 
consideration by the 13th Lok Sabha, and it lapsed. 
The Parliamentary Standing Committee had made 49 
recommendations. The Government have accepted 47 of the 49 
recommendations by making appropriate modifications in the Bill in 
respect of 26 recommendations and incorporating 21   
recommendations in the 
226 

[2 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
rules/regulations which would be framed by the Government and Regulatory 
Board. With respect to the remaining two recommendations relating to 
declaring storage facilities, hydrant systems at airports, etc., as common 
carriers, the Bill introduced in this House on 21" December, 2005 seeks to 
empower the Board to register entities which propose to establish storage 
facilities for petroleum, petroleum products and natural gas beyond a 
certain capacity. The Ministry has generally agreed with the 
recommendations of the entire Committee. 
The Standing Committee had strongly recommended that the 
Government should lay down sepa rate regulations incorporating 
provisions essential to handling the specific problems of the gas 
sector. Our Government fully agrees with this recommendation. The 
petroleum and gas sectors are at different stages of development in the 
country, with the gas sector being at a nascent stage of growth. 
Globally, the share of natural gas in world's primary energy consumption 
is growing faster than the other commercial energy forms. It is often said 
that if oil was the fuel for the 20th century, the 21* century will be the era of 
gas. The Hydrocarbon Vision -2025 projects that the share of natural 
gas in the total energy mix in the country will increase to 20 per cent by 
the year 2025. With a view to incorporating the recommendations of 
the Standing Committee relating to the gas sector in the Bill, the 
Government had extensive consultations with the gas industry and we 
have incorporated appropriate provisions in the Bill, which specifically 
pertain to the gas sector. These relate, inter alia, to: (i) affiliate code of 
conduct; (ii) pipeline access code; ( iii) introduction of the concept of 
contract carrier; (iv) marketing servic e obligations of city or local gas 
distribution entities; (v) exclusivity for ascertain period for building or 
operating city or local gas distribution network; and (vi) methodology for 
fixation of transportation tariffs. 
It may be noted that while the Bill introduced in the Parliament 
in May, 2002 was titled "The Petroleum Regulatory Board pill, 2002", 
the present Bill is "The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board Bill, 
2005". 
In addition to the changes related to the gas sector, a few 
refinements brought about in the present Bill relate to: (i) having a Member 
(Legal or Judicial) on the Board; (if) introduction of the concept of 'restrictive 
trade practices' instead of 'profiteering'; (iii) a common Appellate Tribunal 
for the electricity and petroleum sectors; (iv) deleting the exclusion of the 
jurisdiction of the MRTP Commiss ion/Competition Commission; etc.; 
(v) empowering the Board to register, instead of authorize, the entities 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [2 March, 2006] 
seeking to market petroleum products and setting up Liquefied Natural 
Gas Terminals; and (vi) registration of entities seeking to establish 
storage facilities beyond a certain capacity. 
In respect of laying common or contract carrier pipelines and for 
laying city or local gas distribution networks, the provision of authorization 
by Board has been retained. 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would Ike to convey our thanks to the 
Chairman and Members of the Standing Committee for their 
contribution and valuable suggestions which helped in framing of the Bid, 
and also to the other stakeholders. 
Sir, I now commend the BM to this august House for consideration 
and passing. Thank you.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Benefits to farmers from rising market prices 
*181. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
eased to state: 
(a) whether it Is a fact that farmers are not benefiting from rising market 
ices of wheat as the middlemen are taking all the profits; 
(b) whether Government have a plan to ensure that farmers get adequate 
jnefit from higher market prices of their crops; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): ) to (d) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Marketing of wheat along with other notified commodities is 
gulated under the Agricultural Prod uce Marketing Regulation Act(APMC 
:t). The whole geographical area in the State is divided as market area nerein 
markets are managed by the Market Co mmittees. As a msequence of such a 
regulation, the farmer is restricted from  entering to direct contract with any 
bulk buyer, as the produce is required to be inalized through regulated 
markets. The monopoly of the regulated arket has enabled the intermediaries 
operating therein to take a sproportionate share of the price paid by the 
consumer. As per the 'ailable informa tion, the producer's share in the 
consumer's price in major ieat produci ng States varied between 71.1 % to 
85.72%. The balance is

accounted for by charges such as mandi charges, sales tax, weighing charges, 
palledari, brokerage, transport cost and market margins. 
Government has taken several steps to ensure that the farmers get 
adequate benefit from the higher market  price for their crops. These are as 
follows:— 
(i) This Ministry is proactively en couraging the Stat e Governments to 
promote new competitive markets in private and cooperative sectors 
and ailow direct marketing and contract farming programmes by 
suitabiiy amending APMC Act. This is with the objective of 
promoting fair competition, so that the farmers can gain from the 
options available, and take their produce to the centres that offer the 
best prices/services including regulated markets. 
(ii) This Ministry is implementing a capital investment subsidy scheme 
titled 'Construction of Rural Godowns' w.e.f. 01.04.2001, to provide 
the farming community with facilities for scientific storage so that 
wastage and produce deterioration ar e avoided and also to enable it 
to meet its credit requirement without being compelled to sell the 
produce at a time when the prices  are low. The scheme has been 
made farmer friendly by allowing subsidy for smaller godowns of 
50 MT size in general and of 25 MT in hilly areas. Five lakh tonnes 
capacity to be created is reserved for small farmers. Till 
31.12.2005,10932 storage projects having a capacity of 158.68 lakh 
tonne have been sanctioned under the scheme by providing a 
subsidy of Rs. 279.91 crore. 
(iii) Government his permitted futures trading in wheat at the 
commodity exchange to enable farm ers to discover prices of traded 
commodities including wheat well in advance of the crop season 
thus enabling them to decide when to sell his produce. 
(iv) in addition, to ensure payment of remunerative prices to the farmers, 
the Government announces Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for 
major crops. The price support mechanism enables the farmers to 
sell their produce at remunerative prices, whenever the market 
prices tend to fall below the MSP level.

be HIV positive during hospitalisation at SAT Hospital,

As transfusion of infected blood and blood prodcts is one of the modes of

blood unit is found to be reactive to any of the transfusion transmissible 
infections (HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, Syphilid and Malaria), then the

order to ensure safe supply of blood, professional blood donation has been 
banned in the country since 1st January, 1998. 
One of the principal components of the strategy of ensuring safe blood is 
the promotion of voluntary blood donation. The other activities taken up 
under the programme include modernisation of 1179 blood banks inckftling

practices. The strict enforcement of these measures through training and 
periodic monitoring has enabled transmission of HI V through blood, 
reduced from 9% in 1993 to less than 2% in 2005. The goal of the

Joining the Indian Ocean Tuna Organization 
1177. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAM Y: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that our countr y has joined the Indian Ocean Tuna 
Organization; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the objectives and other salient features of this organization? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOT C) is a Regional Fisheries 
Organization under the Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) of the 
United Nations. This Organization is mandated to manage tuna and tuna like 
species in the Indian Ocean and adj acent seas. India became a member of 
IOTC from the time it came into existence in the year 1996. Tuna and tuna 
like species are highly migratory and straddling in nature, moving between 
the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) of  adjacent countries and the high 
seas. Hence, cooperative efforts are re quired to conserve and manage these 
resources. Since the objective of IOTC is oriented towards management and 
conservation of tuna and allied resources, India has joined this Organization 
for the sustainable development to tuna fisheries in this region through 
cooperative efforts with the member countries. 
(c) The objective of the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission is to review the 
trend of tuna fisheries in the Indian  Ocean and adjacent seas by gathering 
and analyzing scientific information on the resources, maintenance of 
statistics on catch and efforts and maintaining data relevant to the 
conservation and management of the stocks. The Commission is also 
required to coordinate research and development activities in respect of the 
tuna species covered under it and to encourage transfer of technology, 
training of personnel and to address the special interests and needs of the 
member countries. The Commission will promote the objective of optimum 
utilization of the tuna resources based on scientific evidences. At present, 
there are 24 countries represented in the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission and 
the headquarters of the Commission is in Victoria, Seychelles.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) The Seeds Act, 1966 provides the 
framework for regulating quality of certain seeds in the Country Notification 
of a variety is based on the Value for Cultivation and Usage test. Seeds of a 
notified variety can be sold only if they conform to the standards prescribed 
under this Act. The Act also provides for voluntary certification of varieties. 
Certification entails a third party guar antee by an independent agency and 
ensures genetic identity and genetic purity. The Central Seed Committee and 
Central Seed Certification Board an d its various sub committees are the 
agencies set up under the Seeds Act to deal with all matters relating to 
quality control of the seeds. Seed Inspectors notified under the Seeds Act are 
empowered to draw the samples and varify the standards Violation of the 
Seeds Act is a punishable offence. Seed (Control) Order, 1983 another legal 
instrument, has been issued under-the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 in 
order to ensure distribution of quality seeds to the farmers. Seeds (Control) 
Order regulates seed production and distribution. The order provides for 
licensing of seed dealers, the modalities of inspection, sampling, punishment 
of dealers, suspension and cancellati on of licences and has put in place a 
rigorous system of regulation and enforcement. However, the Seed Act and 
the Seed (Control) Order do not apply to farm saved seed.

Essential drugs at cheaper rates 
1210. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will th e Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps Government have taken, so far, to keep its promise of 
providing 354 essential drugs available at cheaper rates as well as to follow 
the Supreme Court's directive to Government that such life-saving drugs do 
not fall out of price control; 
(b) whether Government propose to allocate more budgetary provisions 
during current year as compared to last year in this regard; 
(c) what is the reaction of the Indian Drug Manufacturer Association in 
this regard; and 
(d) the steps Government have taken in this regard in the interest of the 
common man? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) A Committee 
undor the Chairmanship of Joint Secret ary (PI) was constituted to examine 
the span of price control (including trade margin) in the light of National 
Common Minimum Programme and the observations of the Supreme Court 
in SLP No (C) 3668/2003 and to suggest measures for fulfilling the objective 
of National Common Minium Programme to ensure the availability of life 
saving drugs at reasonable prices. This Committee in its interim report 
submitted to the Government has inter-alia recommended that the National 
List of Essential Medicines 2003 should form the basket for identification of 
drugs under price control. Subsequently a Task Force under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen was constituted to explore options other 
than price control to make available lif e saving drugs at reasonable prices. 
The Task Force in its report submitted to the Government on 20.9.05 has 
recommended, inter alia that National List of Essential Medicines containing 
354 items should form the basis of drugs to be considered for intensive price 
monitoring, ceiling prices and imposing price control if any. 
In this regard the Indian Drug Ma nufacturer Association (IDMA) has 
represented mainly for freezing all esse ntial drug prices at current levels, 
automatic increase of price upto 5% per annum, Bulk drugs to be kept out of 
price control, removal of Central Excise and other taxes on all medicines, 
review of Essential list after five years etc.

[3 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The Government, based on the recommendations of the Committee under 
the Chairmanship of Join t Secretary (Pharmaceuticals) and the Task Force 
under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal Advisor, Planning 
Commission, the Government have drafted a National Pharmaceutical 
Policy, 2006 (Part-A), which has been circulated to various stakeholders 
seeking their comments. Based on the comments received the Government is 
likely to finalize the new Policy shortly. 
Some of the salient recommendations  of the national Pharmaceutical 
Policy, 2006 (Part-A), which contains issues other than statutory price 
control pertaining to schemes for pr oviding accessibility of drugs to the 
common man are: 
1) Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana for the BPL families. 
2) Larger allocation would be made for National Illness Assistance Fund. 
3) State Illness Assistance Funds would be set up in all states with 
financial assistance from Central Government. 
4) Revolving Funds for BPL families would be set up in all the Central 
Government hospitals. 
5) States would also be asked to set up revolving funds in all the 
government hospitals for free treatment of BPL families. 
6) In order to increase the reach of po or people to these funds District 
Level Revolving Fund would also be maintained The quantum of the 
District Level Revolving Fund would be Rs. 1.00 crore and this 
amount would bo provided by the Central Government. 
7) Rajasthan model of Medicare Relief Societies to be replicated in all 
the states.

ration card per month with effect from 1.4.2002 and is continuing at the same 
level till date. 
The monthly levy sugar was allotted on the basis of 425 grams per capita 
monthly availability for the projected population as on 1.10.1986 with effect 
from February, 1987. It was revised from January, 1996 onwards ont he basis 
of 425 grams per capita monthly availability for the population as per 1991 
census. From March to July, 2000, the monthly levy sugar quota was based 
on 425 grams per capita monthly availability for the projected population as 
on 1.3.2000. From July, 2000 onwards the monthly levy sugar quota was 
based on 500 grams per capita monthly availability for the projected 
population as on 1.3.2000 and restricting.the allocation of sugar to non-

the monthly levy sugar quota was based on 500 grams per capita monthly 
availability and restricted to people Below Poverty Line (BPL) in non-Hilly

view special circumstances of some States/UTs the levy quota is allotted

registered FIRs against some persons in the Nadia district and some persons 
in North 24 Parganas district who were engaged in preparing fake Elector's 
Photo Identity Cards (EPIC), ration cards  and other certificates. Details of 
such cases are available with the Stat e Government of West Bengal. As the 
ration card is used in many cases as a supporting document (of address 
proof) for the purpose of inclusion of names in electoral rolls, it has been a 
cause for concern of the Commission. The Commission has asked its field 
functionaries to exercise the utmost vigilance in this respect. 
It has been reported by the Food & Supplies Department, Government of 
West Bengal that checking of ration car ds is a regular feature of their work. 
Due to death, transfer of residence, marriage, migration and various factors 
many anomalies creep in and they have  to be regularly eliminated. Special 
drives are also coordinated by the Dist rict Magistrates in West Bengal. The 
total number of expiring ration cards eliminated during the year 2005 in the 
normal process is about 19 lakhs approximately. This checking is an on-
going part of the work. The Food & Supplies Department, Government of 
West Bengal is concerned only with the cards issued by their officers and 
cards (genuine or otherwise) produced before them for checking. 'Fake' cards 
not issued by Food & Supplies Officers and if misused for allegedly 
obtaining EPIC and if detected by Police, cover a series of actions quite 
outside the purview of that Department. The Food & Supplies Department, 
Government of West Bengal do not co ordinate or monitor 'Fake'/Fictitious'

ration wheat and otehr foodgrains has been received;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) The stocks of foodgrains, including wheat, in 
the Central Pool have been adequate and the requirements of Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) and Other Welfare Schemes of all the States are

States regarding some depletion of the stocks: Kerala, Karnataka, Madhya

action and movement to these States was stepped up and the stocks are now 
adequate to meet all the requirements of TPDS and Other Welfare Schemes. 
(c) and (d) It is a regular feature to make movement plan of wheat from 
procuring/surplus States, like Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya 
Pradesh, etc. to the consuming/deficit States to meet the allocation made by 
this Ministry. 
Planning and despatch of the required number of rakes of foodgrains is 
made by the Food Corp oration of India every month for each consuming 
State/UT at an optimally feasible level, within the constraints of availability 
of rakes and other logistics in order to adequately cater to the requirements 
of each States/UT under TPDS and Other Welfare Schemes and with the aim 
of building up and maintaining the stock level equivalent to three months' 
average requirement (two months' in resp ect of N.E. Region). On receipt of 
any report regarding depletion of stocks the Food Corporation of india is 
advised to prioritize the induction of rakes to such States/UT and whenever 
required, the Railway Board is also re quired to take appropriate remedial 
action to augment the supply and induction of the rakes.

Reduction in economic cost of FCI 
1221. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have sought suggestions from some 
organizations during the last two year s to reduce the economic cost of the 
Food corporation of India; 
(b) if so, the names of those organizations alongwith the suggestions 
given by them; and 
(c) the steps taken or proposed to be taken by Government to implement 
those suggestions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) M/s McKinsey & Co. was engaged by the FCI to conduct a 
study to bring about substantial and sustainable efficiency improvements in 
the FCI's functioning, including, inter-alia, recommendations on new 
business models and structural changes, to reduce the subsidy burden while 
improving its effectiveness in meeti ng the Government of India's social 
objectives. M/s McKinsey & Co have submitted their report on 28th July, 
2005. 
The important recommendations made in the report are given in the 
statements (See below). The recommendations are at various stages of 
examination/implementation. To implement the recommendations contained 
in the report, a Programme Implementa tion Office (PIO) has been set up in 
FCI. 
Statement 
The important recommendations made in the report of M/s McKinsey & 
Co. 
(I) Financing Cost Reduction:— 
(a)Advance subsidy release linked to stock holding to reduce 
interest cost. 
(b) Refinancing of buffer stock through issue of bonds. 
104 

[3 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Refinancing of receivables through issue of bonds and/or term 
loan. 
(II) Optimization of rail movement costs by using Linear Programming to 
generate least cost linkages for movement of food grain rakes between 
the source and destination stations. 
(III) Consolidation of handling and transport contracts to reap the benefit of 
economies of scale. 
(IV) Renting out/De-hiring of excess shortage capacity. 
(V) Reduction of gunny costs by using once used gunny for procurement 
of paddy and by making purchase through open tender. 
 
(VI) Reduction of procurement cost by Direct Procurement. 
(VII) Reduction in Arthiya Commission, Purchase tax and other statutary 
chajrge. 
(VIII) Reduction of Establishment cost by rationalised deployment of 
manpower & outsourcing of non-critical activities such as security, 
housekeeping etc. 
(IX) Improving efficiency by implementing a management Information 
System that tracks key performan ce indicators and provides accurate 
operational data necessary for effective decision making. 
 
(X) Reduction of Labour cost by Increasing handling norms, 
Redistribution labour across depots for better match of handling load 
and labour availability, identifying surplus labour and developing 
targeted VRS & preventing departmentalization of DPS and Contract 
Labour. 
(XI) Advance payment to state agencies against Central pool procurement 
to reduce interest cost.

AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) The Targ etted Public Distribution System

efficiency, accountability and effectiveness is an ongoing process. Besides 
notification of the Public Distribution System (Control) Order, 2001, 
involvement of the Panchayati Raj Institutions, model citizen's charter and

monitor the TPDS and the Antyodaya Anna Yojana, conferences of State 
Food Secretaries, State Food Ministers, meeting witb All India Fair Price 
Shops Dealers Federation and a meeting with all the Members of Parliament 
was organized for strengthening of TPDS and to make th system more 
successful. Regional Conferences have been held with focus on the unique 
problems of the region and to facilitate strengthening of the TPDS in a 
manner, which may be relevant to the local environment. Innovative steps 
like issue of bar-coded coupons, involvement of self-help groups, 
particularly of women, setting up of vigilance committees at FPS level have 
been adopted by various state governments to ensure correct distribution of 
foodgrains.

1225. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the incidence of subsidies on ite ms meant for Below Poverty Line 
(BPL) population in the country; 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2009] 
(b) whether the distribution of subsidized items is done through the public 
distribution system; and 
(c) whether a large amount of subsidies are going to the mills/factories 
where such items are value-added? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) Under Targ eted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS), foodgrains (rice & wheat) and s ugar are distributed for the families 
below poverty line (BPL). Subsidies are also given on domestic LPG and 
PDS Kerosene irrespective of whether the consumer belongs to BPL family 
or not. 
Foodgrains: 
Subsidised foodgrains (rice & wheat ) for the BPL families are issued 
under TPDS at the central issue prices of Rs. 565 per quintal for rice and Rs. 
415 per quintal for wheat through fair price shops all over the country. Some 
States have entrusted the work to Co-operatives. 
Sugar: 
The Government has restructured the public distribution system in respect 
of sugar with effect from 1.2.2001, under which the supply of levy sugar has 
been restricted to only BPL families except in the North Eastern States, Hilly 
States and Island Territories. Sugar is issued at Rs. 13.20 per kilogram under 
PDS. 
LPG and Kerosene: 
The distribution of domestic LPG is not made through the PDS but distf 
tbution of PDS kerosene is done through PDS. 
(c) An evaluation study of Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) 
conducted by the Planning Commission co vering eighteen major States has 
observed that out of the subsidized foodgrains under the TPDS there is 
leakage of about 19.71 percent at Fair Price Shops (FPS) level and about 
16.67 per cent of the foodgrains is diverted through ghost cards. In addition, 
the TPDS suffers from diversion of subsidized grains to unintended 
beneficiaries (above poverty line (APL) households) because of errors of 
inclusion. However, the report is based on old primary data of 2001-2002. 
As several changes like introduction of Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY), 
change in the scale of issue, etc. have  taken place since then, it is difficult to 
totally rely on this report.

randomly from the birds and are being sent to High Security Animal Disease 
Laboratory, Bhopal. Besides the samples from Navapur, Maharshtra and 
Uchchal, Gujarat, none of the samples have been tested positive for Avian

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) Sex ratio in India has declined over the 
century from 972 in 1901 to 927 in 1991. The sex ratio has since gone up to 
933 in 2001. In contrast the child sex ratio for the age group of 0-6 years in 
2001 in 927 girls per thousand boys against 945 recorded in 1991 Census. 
(b) Some of the reasons commonly put forward to explain the 
consistently low levels of sex ratio are son preference, low value of girl 
child, neglect of girl child resulting in higher mortality at younger age, 
female infanticide, femalo foeticide,  higher childhood mortality and male 
bias in enumeration of population. 
(c) Imbalance in the sex-ratio may lead to further decline in the status of 
women, increase in violence against women practices of polyandry etc. 
(d) Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has undertaken training of 
trainers from State Judicial Academie s to train lower judiciary with the 
objective to'sensitize th e judiciary on the issue. National Inspection and 
Monitoring Committee (NIMC) having representatives of Department of 
Women & Child Development, National Commission for Women, Indian 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [3 March, 2006] 
Council for Medical Research as member s, undertakes periodical visits to 
the districts with low child sex ratio (0-6 years) to oversee the 
implementation of the Act at ground level and monitors the prosecutions 
launched against unregistered bodies and bodies violating provisions of the 
Act/Rules and directions of the Suprem e Court of India in the matter. The 
National Support and Monitoring Cell is being constituted as a mechanism 
to help Appropriate Authorities in apprehending the wrong doer who are 
committing female foeticide/abetting female foeticide. 
It is, however, recognized that mere legislation is not enough to deal with 
thir. problem that has roots in social behavior and prejudices. A number of 
activities to create awareness on th e issue are being undertaken. The 
initiatives include meeting with the organizations working against sex 
selection, involvement of the medical professionals, religions leaders to 
spread the message, requesting police training academies and schools to 
include the issues in curriculum of th eir training, telecasting of video spots 
on private satellite channels and Doordarshan, and involvement of elected 
representatives etc. A 'Save the Girl Child" Campaign with a view to lessen 
son preference by highlighting achievements of young girls has been 
launched. District Magistrates have also been requested to regularly review 
the implementation of the Pre-concepticn and Pre-natal Diagnostic 
Techniques Act along with other health programmes in their district.

countries as well. 
The amended Schedule Y mandates that Ethics Committees review 
"Insurance Policy/Compensation for participation and for serious adverse 
events occurring during the study participation." 
The informed consent checklist under Schedule Y also prescribes that the 
patient should be informed by clinician (Investigator) about "Compensation 
and/or treatment (s) available to the Subject in the event of a trial-related 
injury." 
According to India Good Clinical Practices (GCP) Guidelines, which 
must be complied with as per Schedule Y, the sponsor is responsible to 
indemnify and obtain insurance to cover the cost of treatment in case of any 
study related harm to patients, and also to provide compensation as 
prescribed by the laws of the land.

standard of loading than prevalent, i.e., there has been tremendous growth of 
load both in freight as well as passe nger traffic since the construction of

section, thorough study is carried out for suitability of existing bridges. If 
required, bridges are rehabilitated/rebuilt to hear the heavier axle load of 
freight/passenger trains.

well laid down system of multi-tier inspection of bridges is followed in the 
Indian Railways. The rehabilitation/ rebuilding of the bridges is carried out 
based on the physical condition as ascer tained during inspection and not on 
the basis of age alone. In case a section is selected for introduction of heavier 
loads, all the bridges of that section are reviewed and strengthened as per 
requirement.

Increase in rail accidents 
†1317. SHRIJANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the numb er of train accidents has increase 
during the last two years; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that  the reason behind these accidents is 
misuse of modem technique by the employees; 
(c) if so, whether Government have taken any steps to minimize the train 
accidents and also to check the misuse  of modern techni que by employees; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (d) No, Sir. Safety is the prime concern of Indian 
Railways and all possible steps are undertaken on a continuing basis to 
prevent accidents. These measures incl ude timely replacement of over aged 
assets, adoption of suitable technologies for upgradation and maintenance of 
track, rolling stock, signaling and interlocking systems, safety drives and 
inspections at regular Intervals to monitor and educate staff for observance 
of safe practices. As a result the number of consequential train accidents 
have come down from 473 in 2002-2001 to 415 in 2001 -2002,351 in 2002-
2003,325 in 2003-2004, and further to 234 in 2004-05.

GOVERNMENT BILL 
The contempt of courts (Amendment) Bill, 2006 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Contempt of Courts Act, 
1971, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration." 
(THE VICE-CHAIRMAN, (SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA) in the Chair) 
Sir, I would like to make a brief comment before I request the House 
to take up this Bill. The House is awar e that the existing provisions of the 
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 has been interpreted by various courts and 
judicial decisions to the effect that truth cannot be treated  as a defence to a 
charge of contempt of court. It was the law. Therefore, after a lot of 
discussions in the legal and judicial circle s, it was thought that there is room 
to amend this law and make the truth one of the valid defence. Some eminent 
jurists expressed their views and wrote ar ticles also, and suggested that the 
truth can be a very valid defence subject to the court permitting it. 
I am also happy to inform that the previous Government started this 
task and the matter was referred to the National Commission to Review the 
Working of the Constitution. The Constitution Review Committee, headed by 
hon. Justice Venkatachaliah, inter alia, recommended that in matters of 
contempt it shall be open to the Court to  permit a defence of justification by 
truth. The Government has been advised  that amendments to the Contempt 
of Courts Act, 1971 to provide for the above provision would introduce 
fairness in procedure and meet the requirements of article 21 of the 
Constitution. So, Sir, Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971    
provides   certain   circumstances   under   which   contempt   is   not

SHRIMATI N. P. OURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I rise to support the 
Contempt of Courts (Amendment) Bid,  2006. Mr, as per the Contempt of 
Courts Act, 1971 if anybody scandalises or lowers the authority of any court 
or interferes with the course of any ju dicial proceedings, he is Sable to be 
punished for criminal contempt and, if there is a wilful disobedience to any 
judgment, decree, direction, order or writ, it is a civil contempt. 
The contempt of court represents a range of offences and those can 
be divided into three broad categories. The first on* it contempt of publication. 
The second one is contempt by disobedience and the third one is contempt in 
the face of the court. 
Sir, there are two main reasons to confer the power on the courts to 
punish people for contempt.  The first one is that the courts should be 
341 

RAJYA SABHA       [3 March, 2006] 
armed with the power to enforce their orders. Secondly, they should be able 
to punish obstruction to the administration of justice. We have imported this 
contempt of court from the British ju risprudence. In Britain, the Law of 
Contempt was evolved by judges themse lves. Later on, they expanded their 
own powers to punish people for acts of scandalising the court. We have 
imported exactly this very phrase from British and put it under Section 2 of the 
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. So, any im putation of dishonesty to judges or 
their judgments is regarded as contempt. 
Recently, the Law of Contempt has  been liberalised in the United 
States of America and the United Kingd om. In the United Kingdom, it was 
liberalised on the recommendations of  the Phillimore Committee to provide 
truth as a defence to a charge of c ontempt. So, India has also started 
amending its Contempt of Court. This cl early shows that the influence of the 
British is still there on our judiciary. 
Coming to the Bill, I would say that, according to the existing 
provision, even the truth of imputation could not be pleaded in defence. Thus, 
if one called a judge dishonest and had evidence to prove it, the courts would 
not allow it on the ground that such an im putation, even if true, would impair 
public confidence in the administration of  justice. The proposed BHi, to some 
extent, covers this because you are inserting a clause, which permits the truth 
as a valid defence. But there is a rider.  The rider is that it should be in the 
public interest. I would like to know what is public interest. The word has a 
very wide meaning. Nowhere, it has  been mentioned as to what constitutes 
public interest. 
The other point I would like to know from the hon. Minister is this. Sir, 
the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution 
recommended the amendment of the Cont empt of Courts Act, since the 
inherent powers of contempt were ve sted with the Supreme Court and the 
High Courts. But, in the Pritam Lai case , the Supreme Court had said that its 
powers of contempt could not be rest ricted by any ordinary legislation, 
including the Contempt of Courts Act. In  the light of this ruling, how is the 
Government going to justify the propos ed amendment? Is it going to bring 
amendment to the relevant articles -- articles 129 to 142 -- so as to set aside 
the judgement of the Court in the Pritam Lai Case? I request the hon. Minister 
to reply to this question. 
Finally, Sir, I would say that there are inconsistencies in looking at 
and deciding the contempt cases.   For example, the Supreme Court in the

Chief Justice of India. At the same ti me, there were others similarly placed 
who were either ignored or got away with just having been reprimanded. Dr. 
Kiran Bedi committed contempt of court when she failed to submit an 
undertrial's medical report to the Supreme Court. A former Law Minister

is unable to understand as to which on e amounts to contempt of court. Even 
in England the Contempt law has hardly been used for more than the last

Speaking on the-use of this Law, Lord Denning observed, "Let me 
say, at once, that we will never use this jurisdiction as a means to uphold our 
own dignity". If such power is necessary for preserving the public confidence 
in the judiciary, then the same argument would hold good for preserving 
confidence in the Government, its bureaucracy and police. After all, these are 
also performing public functions and it is equally important for their efficacy 
that public confidence in them should also be preserved. So, I would suggest 
that the best check against their degener ation was their accountability to the 
people for which it was essential that the people should have the right to 
freely comment on them and criticise them. 
So, I would suggest that the Government should streamline or 
repeal this outdated piece of legislati on to protect the freedom of speech and 
expression provided under article 19 of the Constitution to every citizen.

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Mr. Deputy Chairman, 
Sir, I move: 
That the Bill to eliminate the discrim ination against the girl child by 
providing for the equal upbringing and remove of neglect by her 
parents or guardians and violation of her rights by marrying her off 
during her childhood and forcing her in begging, prostitution and 
other crimes by providing deterrent  punishment for such violations 
and for welfare measures such as free and compulsory education 
including vocational education enabling her to enjoy her childhood 
and for matters connected therewith and incidental thereto, be taken 
into consideration.

majority of the families of our nation who prefer to eliminate even the foetus if 
it is of a girl child. Thousands of legal or illegal ultrasound clinics are 
functioning in the country, which are in famous as pre-birth sex determination 
test clinics. As happens in our Indian  households, everybody wants a male 
baby and for this the services of the sex determination clinics are taken. If the 
foetus is that of a female, it is abor ted as soon as possible. For this the 
consent of the mother is neither taken nor it is respected. In some cases, it is 
the mother who decides to eliminate the female foetus. This is common not 
only in illiterate poor families  but it is more in educated and affluent families. 
In western countries, ultrasound is used to find out the deformity in the child 
to safeguard the child as well as t he mother, but here in India they use 
ultrasound clinics-to find out whether it is  a female foetus so that Itt can be 
aborted. Though prenatal se x determination is illegal in the country, but who 
bothers about the law. This  profitable nefarious bus iness is increasing by 
leap and bounds resulting in steep decline in male-female ratio in the 
country, particularly in the northern and western regions of the country. 
Sir, today, 16 States, more specific ally, 70 districts and 23 cities in 
the country, have a shocking sex ratio. If this is not taken seriously, 15 years 
later, the effect of what we see today will surface as a social unrest.

*203. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of registered units of small scale industries in the country upto the 
31st December, 2005, State-wise and Union Territory-wise; 
(b) how many of these are in running condition and how many have been 
closed; 
(c) the reasons for such a big number of units having been closed; 
(d) the number of workers having lost their work; and 
(e) the steps taken to check failures upto such an extent? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHAVIR 
PRASAD): (a) to (e) A statement is placed on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) According to the information received from the Directorates of 
Industries of States/Union Territories, the estimated total number of SSI units 
registered all over the country upto 31 December 2005 was 18,41,248. The State-wise 
and Union Territory-wise break-up of these registered small scale industries is given 
in the enclosed Statement-I (see below). 
(b) The information on closed small scale industries has not been collected 
by the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations or the Central 
Government after the Third All India Census (2002-03) of small scale 
industries. According to the results of that Census, 39 per cent of small scale 
industries registered upto 31 Ma rch 2001 were found closed during 
enumeration. 
(c) Fall, in demand for the products of SSI units, use of outdated 
technology, difficulty in availability of working capital and raw materials, 
constraints in electricity supply a nd other infrastructure, management 
inadequacies, etc., are some of the main reasons of closure of these units. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2008] 
(d) The data on the number of work ers rendered jobless due to closure 
of SSIs are not maintained at the Cents a! level. 
(e) The respective State Governments and 'he Union Territory 
Administrations are primarily responsible for the promotion and development 
of SSIs. However, several policy deci sions have been taken and several 
schemes/programmes are implemented by the Central Government for 
the development and promotion of SSI. Among them, ensuring availability 
of credit through public sector financial institutions (including banks), 
technology upgradation, marketing assistance, integrated infrastructural 
development, etc., are important. 
The Government has announced a "Policy Package for Stepping up of Credit 
to Small and Medium Enterprises" on 10 August 2005. Based on this, the 
Reserve Bank of India has issued detailed guidelines to the banks regarding 
restructuring/rehabilitation of sick small enterprises.

SHRIMATI KAMLA MANHAR:

charged by private institutions/schools in Delhi; and

structure of private institutions/schools in Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) Improvement of 
educational standards is a continuous process. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Teacher

Vidyalayas are the major schemes be ing implemented, among others, for 
qualitative improvement of school education, Besides, the National Curriculum 
Framework for School Education has been revised in 2005 with improvement of 
quality as the main focus. University Grants Commission and All India Council 
for Technical Education (AICTE) look after the aspects of standard and quality in 
higher and technical education, respectively.

every recognized school shall, before the commencement of each academic 
session, file with the Director a full statement of the fee to be levied by such 
school during the ensuing academic session, and except with the prior approval 
of the Director, no such school shall charge, during the academic session, any fee in 
excess of the fee specified by its manager in the said statement.

Territory Administrations.
